cases.decision_text: Any package author may unpublish any version of their own package at any time, with no check on who else depends on it (npm's registry behavior through March 2016).

options.text: Keep unpublish unrestricted: any author may remove any version of their own package at any time.
options.source: npm registry behavior as described in npm's own postmortem: "Unrestricted un-publishing caused a lot of pain." (blog.npmjs.org/post/141577284765, 2016-03-23)

options.text: Restrict unpublish: allow free unpublish only within a short window after publish; after that, require npm support to check who depends on the package before removing it.
options.source: npm's own stated need, same postmortem: "npm needs safeguards to keep anyone from causing so much disruption. If these had been in place yesterday, this post-mortem wouldn't be necessary." (blog.npmjs.org/post/141577284765, 2016-03-23)

incident.text: Azer Kocjulu unpublished 273 packages including left-pad (11 lines, ~2.5M downloads/month) after npm transferred the disputed package name 'kik' to Kik Interactive. Babel, Atom and thousands of dependent projects failed within minutes because a transitive dependency (line-numbers) pinned the exact version left-pad@0.0.3. npm restored the original 0.0.3 from backup after 2.5 hours of outage, an operation the registry does not normally support.

cases.ground_truth_source: npm, "Changes to npm's unpublish policy" (blog.npmjs.org/post/141905368000, 2016-03-29): unpublish restricted to packages <24h old (later widened to 72h, 2020-01-30); older packages require contacting support, which checks dependents; a fully-removed package name is replaced by a security placeholder. The npm-unpublish-unrestricted decision is REVERSED/SUPERSEDED by npm-unpublish-windowed.
cases.trigger_to_decision_link: scope: npm registry unpublish behavior; decision: directly named in both postmortem and policy-change posts (same npm, Inc. author, izs/Laurie Voss, within one week).

cases.decision_text: Every GitHub Actions workflow run is issued a GITHUB_TOKEN with read AND write permissions across repository scopes by default, with no opt-in required (GitHub Actions behavior 2019-2023 for repos not explicitly reconfigured).

options.text: Keep GITHUB_TOKEN defaulting to read/write: maximizes convenience for workflows that push commits, tags, releases, or packages without per-workflow configuration.
options.source: GitHub Changelog, "GitHub Actions - Updating the default GITHUB_TOKEN permissions to read-only" (github.blog/changelog/2023-02-02-...): "Previously, GitHub Actions gets a GITHUB_TOKEN with both read/write permissions by default whenever Actions is enabled on a repository. As a default, this is too permissive" (GitHub's own retrospective framing of the prior default).

options.text: Default GITHUB_TOKEN to read-only; workflows that need write access must opt in explicitly via the permissions: block.
options.source: GitHub Security Lab blog, "How to secure GitHub Actions workflows": "these tokens originally had a very broad set of permissions ... today, the default permissions for new repositories and organizations are set to read-only" (github.blog/security/supply-chain-security/four-tips...); principle-of-least-privilege framing is GitHub's own.

incident.date: 2023 (Palo Alto Networks Unit42/GitHub Security Lab research; the read-only default itself shipped 2023-02-02, concurrent with this published supply-chain research)
incident.text: Security researchers (Palo Alto Networks) demonstrated a worm using a write-permissioned GITHUB_TOKEN to push malicious commits or tags into dependent repositories through the Actions dependency tree, escalating a single compromised Action into a self-propagating supply-chain attack across public repos; GitHub's own Security Lab cites the same write-by-default token as the exploited precondition.

cases.ground_truth_source: GitHub Changelog, 2023-02-02: new enterprises/orgs/repos get a read-only GITHUB_TOKEN by default going forward; existing repos keep read/write (grandfathered) but can opt in to read-only. gh-token-default-readwrite is REVERSED (for new scopes) by gh-token-default-readonly.
cases.trigger_to_decision_link: scope: GitHub Actions GITHUB_TOKEN default permission; both the incident research and the changelog entry name the same mechanism (write-by-default token) as cause and fix.

cases.decision_text: A StopIteration raised accidentally inside a generator function (not via a normal return) propagates out and is interpreted by the driving loop/next() caller as ordinary, silent end-of-iteration (CPython behavior before PEP 479).

options.text: Keep StopIteration propagating silently out of a generator frame: minimal, long-standing behavior, no backwards-incompatible change.
options.source: PEP 479 Background/Rationale (peps.python.org/pep-0479, accepted 2014-11-22): describes this as "currently somewhat surprising, and can conceal obscure bugs" -- PEP 479's own framing of the status quo it argues against.

options.text: If a StopIteration is about to bubble out of a generator frame, replace it with RuntimeError so the failure is loud, not silently treated as iteration end.
options.source: PEP 479 Proposal section (peps.python.org/pep-0479): "If a StopIteration is about to bubble out of a generator frame, it is replaced with RuntimeError" -- the PEP's own accepted text.

incident.text: A generator wrapped by a context manager (contextlib.contextmanager) using yield from silently swallowed a StopIteration raised inside the wrapped block, skipping finalization without any error -- a subtle, hard-to-debug failure mode the PEP's own worked example reproduces exactly (a transaction() context manager whose commit/rollback logic is silently skipped). The same class of bug affects asyncio coroutines and bare next() calls on an unexpectedly empty iterator.
incident.source: PEP 479, Rationale section, worked `transaction()`/`do_it()` example and "[2]" footnote referencing "the one that started this discussion" (peps.python.org/pep-0479, fetched 2026-11-08).

cases.ground_truth_source: PEP 479, Acceptance section: "This PEP was accepted by the BDFL on November 22[, 2014]." Status: Final, shipped as the default behavior starting Python 3.7. py-stopiteration-propagates is REVERSED by PEP 479's accepted behavior.
cases.trigger_to_decision_link: scope: CPython generator frame StopIteration handling; the PEP's own Rationale section is simultaneously the incident report and the decision record (single real document, both roles).
